title: Making a furin site isn't hard at all — admitting it isn't rare is
dek: Deep sequencing shows that a few genomes in every thousand carry an insertion, and a furin site has been hit independently at the same position at least three times — the probabilistic argument for a lab origin doesn't hold up.
why: The first half is the quantitative methodology of viral recombination and insertion; the second half is the real target of this episode: dismantling the lab-origin argument with numbers. Listeners who want the argument can jump straight to 52 minutes.
who: Readers interested in viral evolution, the lab-origin debate, and deep-sequencing methodology; anyone who wants to see a controversy taken apart with quantitative data rather than rhetoric.
skip: The chat about fake olive oil and contact lenses after 1:41 at the end has nothing to do with the science.

points.h: They changed the GFP sequence and the recombination rate went up
points.body: The team first built an OC43 reverse-genetics system and made a pair of viruses: each carried a frameshifted GFP, so infection alone produced only fragments, but coinfection followed by recombination could stitch green fluorescent protein back together. They expected that changing the nucleotide sequence of one of the GFPs would lower the recombination rate; instead it rose. Paul says there is only a hypothesis for this, no data — one possibility is that once double-stranded RNA forms, the strand-transfer events of recombination become more likely because the duplex "breathes." This counterintuitive result later became the reagent starting point for the whole paper.

points.h: Knock GFP out of frame and let insertions reveal themselves
points.body: Measuring insertions and deletions is far harder than measuring point mutations, because they were thought to be rare and sequencing depth was insufficient. Their approach was to put the GFP gene into the viral genome and then deliberately knock it out of frame, preceded by a start-codon peptide that is in a different frame from GFP, so the virus does not glow green; it turns green only when that site acquires an insertion or deletion of a particular length that pulls GFP back into frame. This lets them both count event frequencies and pick out green viruses to sequence and infer the mechanism. This is where figure 1 of the paper comes from.

points.h: Knocking out NSP15 made insertions go down, not up
points.body: The original hypothesis came from prior work suggesting that NSP15, a nuclease, affects deletion rates — think nuclease and you naturally think deletions, not insertions. But the experiment went the other way: viruses with NSP15 showed a greatly increased rate of acquiring insertions that pulled GFP back into frame. Paul says the deletion rate numbers were not good enough this time to quantify, but the insertion result was black and white, and they were very surprised at the time; it was this accidental result that opened up the whole line of research.

points.h: Every base sequenced a million times before you talk frequency
points.body: They moved from picking green viruses to brute-force sequencing: concentrating about 10 milliliters of virus down to 1 milliliter, loading part of it onto a sequencing chip, and producing hundreds of millions of reads, so that every nucleotide in the genome was sequenced at least a million times, with roughly 30 human genomes' or 3 million viral genomes' worth of data per virus stock. Paul stresses that depth has to match the number of virions in the sample — sequencing hundreds of millions of times when there are only a thousand virions in the tube is meaningless; they calibrated to sequence roughly a few percent of the viruses in the sample.

points.h: Eleven nucleotides is the threshold for judging origin
points.body: Short insertions (three to six nucleotides) can arise randomly in a viral genome, so their origin cannot be determined, and they were excluded from the analysis. They calculated that if an 11-nucleotide stretch perfectly matches the viral genome, the probability of that being pure chance is below 5%, so they restricted the analysis to insertions of 11 nucleotides or more. The result: over 90% matched the viral genome perfectly or nearly perfectly, and in OC43 wild-type virus had 87 times more insertions than the NSP15 mutant, most of them derived from the positive strand.

points.h: Insertions aren't rare events — they're a few per thousand
points.body: Vincent says he was told for years that insertions are rare, but the data suggest this has been happening all along. Paul responds that "rare" is a relative term: one in a million is rare, but if you have ten million of them, it's common. The insertion frequency they report is a few genomes per thousand — roughly five to ten genomes carrying an insertion out of a thousand virions. That frequency is lower than the point-mutation rate, but not by much. The reason it seemed rare in the past is that the vast majority of insertions are harmful or even lethal to the virus and get purged at low multiplicity of infection, so you can't isolate them.

points.h: Making a furin site isn't hard at all
points.body: Mechanistically, a furin cleavage site needs at minimum two arginines, RXXR, and can even be cleaved with a single arginine plus other amino acids cooperating. Six of the 64 codons encode arginine, and multiplying the two fractions together, about 1% of random 12-base sequences encode an RXR motif. There are roughly 30,000 different positions in a coronavirus genome where an insertion mutation can occur. So this is not some enormous engineering challenge.

points.h: Lightning strikes the same spot at least three times
points.body: Putting the insertion frequency, the number of insertable sites, and the viral population size together, the probability of a furin cleavage site appearing at one particular position in a coronavirus genome is not astonishing, and it roughly matches what deep sequencing actually measures. In their deep-sequencing data, which does not cover the whole population, they have already found new furin cleavage sites at least three independent times at the exact position of SARS-CoV-2's existing furin site. Paul says the numbers in the paper are an underestimate: they only did PCR focused on the spike region, and they required insertions to match the viral genome perfectly to rule out PCR artifacts, which very likely also excluded some real natural sites.

points.h: Every dominant variant started as a single RNA molecule
points.body: Delta, Omicron, every dominant variant, nearly every sequence in the world, began as a single RNA molecule in someone's lung at some point in time. A single event, however improbable, is enough to set off a global transmission chain. So arguments based on "the probability of something happening is extremely low" don't hold up — everything that happens in biology is extremely rare. Paul also points out that the furin cleavage site is not always advantageous for SARS-CoV-2; in many cell-culture experiments the virus is selected to lose the site, and the stability and fusogenicity of the spike trimer are probably balanced on a knife's edge.

points.h: A mouse gene sequence spells out SARS ass
points.body: A PNAS paper by Harrison and Saxs argued for a laboratory origin of SARS-CoV-2 and listed the furin cleavage site of the epithelial sodium channel studied at UNC as a possible insertion candidate. But the amino acid sequence of that mouse epithelial sodium channel furin site spells out exactly "SARS ass." Paul says they glossed over the fact that half of that candidate sequence already exists in other sarbecoviruses.
